It complements the general overview of the program by giving the dates, crews, spacecraft names, landing sites and durations that distinguish each mission from the others. Apollo 7 was the first crewed flight of the Apollo spacecraft. It lifted off on October 11, 1968, and stayed in Earth orbit until splashdown on October 22, 1968, a flight of roughly ten days and twenty hours. The crew was Wally Schirra, Donn Eisele, and Walter Cunningham. Because the rocket was the smaller Saturn IB, the mission never left low Earth orbit. Its purpose was to prove that the command and service module could keep a crew alive for a long flight and that its main engine could be restarted many times. The mission did include the first live television broadcasts from an American crewed spacecraft. Apollo 8 followed in December 1968 and was a bold change of plan. It launched on December 21, 1968, aboard a Saturn V and carried Frank Borman, Jim Lovell, and William Anders to the Moon without a lunar module. The crew became the first humans to travel to the Moon and the first to see the far side of it with their own eyes. They completed ten orbits of the Moon over about twenty hours. On the fourth orbit Anders photographed the Earth rising above the lunar horizon, an image that became known as Earthrise. On Christmas Eve the crew read

On Christmas Eve the crew read verses from the Book of Genesis in a television broadcast watched by a very large audience. Apollo 8 returned to Earth on December 27, 1968, splashing down in the Pacific Ocean. Apollo 9 flew from March 3 to March 13, 1969, and tested the lunar module for the first time with a crew aboard. The astronauts were James McDivitt, David Scott, and Russell Schweickart, and the whole flight stayed in Earth orbit. The command module was named Gumdrop and the lunar module was named Spider. Because the lunar module had spindly legs and no aerodynamic shape, it could only fly in the vacuum of space, and the name Spider seemed fitting. Schweickart performed a spacewalk to test the portable life support backpack that the Moon walkers would later use. Apollo 10 was the full dress rehearsal for the landing. It flew from May 18 to May 26, 1969, with Thomas Stafford, John Young, and Eugene Cernan aboard. The command module was called Charlie Brown and the lunar module was called Snoopy. Stafford and Cernan took Snoopy down to an altitude of about 15.6 kilometers above the lunar surface, close enough to photograph the planned Apollo 11 landing site in the Sea of Tranquility, while Young remained in orbit in the command module. It launched on November 14, 1969, in rain, and the Saturn V was struck by lightning twice during the first minute of flight. Several instruments went dark, but a flight controller suggested switching a signal conditioning unit to its auxiliary setting, the crew did so, and the mission continued. The crew was Charles "Pete" Conrad, Alan Bean, and Richard Gordon. Conrad and Bean landed the lunar module Intrepid in the Ocean of Storms on November 19, 1969, while Gordon orbited in the command module Yankee Clipper. Duke left a family photograph on the surface. The extended lunar module flown on Apollo 15 to 17 had larger propellant tanks, more batteries, and extra oxygen and water, which made the three-day stays possible. The Apollo program was run by NASA from 1961 to 1972 with the goal of landing humans on the Moon. President John F. Kennedy announced the goal in a speech to Congress in May 1961, saying the United States should land a man on the Moon and return him safely to Earth before the end of the decade. Apollo 11 launched on July 16, 1969, from Kennedy Space Center in Florida atop a Saturn V rocket. The crew was Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, and Michael Collins. Armstrong and Aldrin landed the lunar module, named Eagle, in the Sea of Tranquility on July 20, 1969. Collins stayed in lunar orbit aboard the command module Columbia. Neil Armstrong was the first person to step onto the lunar surface. Buzz Aldrin followed about 19 minutes later. The two astronauts spent roughly two and a half hours outside the lunar module, collecting about 21.5 kilograms of lunar rock and soil samples and deploying

and a half hours outside the lunar module, collecting about 21.5 kilograms of lunar rock and soil samples and deploying scientific instruments. The Saturn V was the rocket that carried Apollo astronauts toward the Moon. It stood 110.6 meters tall and remains the most powerful rocket to have flown successfully. It had three stages: the S-IC first stage, the S-II second stage, and the S-IVB third stage, which fired twice to send the spacecraft toward the Moon. Apollo 13 launched in April 1970 and was meant to be the third lunar landing. An oxygen tank in the service module exploded about two days into the flight, forcing the crew of Jim Lovell, Jack Swigert, and Fred Haise to abandon the landing. They used the lunar module Aquarius as a lifeboat and returned safely to Earth on April 17, 1970. The Apollo program had six successful crewed Moon landings: Apollo 11, 12, 14, 15, 16, and 17.

Eugene Cernan was the last person to walk on the Moon. Twelve astronauts in total walked on the lunar surface. Apollo 1 ended in tragedy on January 27, 1967, when a cabin fire during a launch rehearsal killed astronauts Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee. The fire led to major redesigns of the spacecraft, including a new hatch and a switch away from a pure oxygen atmosphere on the launch pad. Apollo 15, 16, and 17 carried the lunar roving vehicle, an electric car that let astronauts travel several kilometers from the lunar module. The total cost of the Apollo program was about 25.4 billion dollars at the time, which is roughly 250 billion dollars in modern currency.

Three ways to fix carbon: C3, C4, and CAM photosynthesis All green plants use the Calvin cycle to turn carbon dioxide into sugar, but they differ in how carbon dioxide reaches the cycle. Plants are grouped into three types according to the way they handle this first step: C3, C4, and CAM. The names refer to the number of carbon atoms in the first stable product, or in the case of CAM, to Crassulacean acid metabolism, a pathway first studied in members of the stonecrop family, Crassulaceae. The differences are mostly adaptations to heat, bright light, and water shortage, and they help to explain why certain plants dominate certain climates. C3 photosynthesis is the original and most common pathway. About 85 percent of plant species use it, including rice, wheat, barley, soybeans, potatoes, and nearly all trees. In a C3 plant, carbon dioxide that enters through the stomata is picked up

RuBisCO attaches the carbon dioxide to a five-carbon sugar called ribulose bisphosphate, and the resulting six-carbon compound immediately splits into two molecules of the three-carbon acid 3-phosphoglycerate. Because this is the first stable product and has three carbons, the pathway is called C3. All of the reactions of the Calvin cycle occur in the stroma of the chloroplasts in the same cells. C3 plants have a weakness, which is that RuBisCO can also react with oxygen instead of carbon dioxide. When it does, the plant wastes energy and releases carbon dioxide in a process called photorespiration. The tendency for oxygen to compete with carbon dioxide rises with temperature, because warm leaves hold

hotorespiration. The tendency for oxygen to compete with carbon dioxide rises with temperature, because warm leaves hold less dissolved carbon dioxide relative to oxygen, and because plants close their stomata on hot days, which causes carbon dioxide inside the leaf to fall and oxygen to build up. In hot weather, photorespiration can cut the efficiency of a C3 plant by a quarter or more. C3 plants therefore do best in cool, moist climates with moderate light, with an optimum temperature of roughly 15 to 25 degrees Celsius, and their photosynthesis levels off at moderate light intensities. C4 photosynthesis is an adaptation that largely avoids photorespiration. Researchers Marshall Hatch and Charles Slack described the pathway in the mid-1960s, and it is sometimes called the Hatch-Slack pathway. The key to C4 photosynthesis is a division of labor between two kinds of cells. The leaves of C4 plants have a special wreath-like arrangement known as Kranz anatomy, in which a ring of bundle sheath cells surrounds each vein, and these are in turn surrounded by mesophyll cells. In the mesophyll cells, carbon dioxide is first captured by an enzyme called PEP carboxylase, not by RuBisCO. PEP carboxylase attaches carbon dioxide, in the form of bicarbonate, to a three-carbon molecule called phosphoenolpyruvate, producing the four-carbon acid oxaloacetate. Because the first stable product has four carbons, the pathway is called

e, producing the four-carbon acid oxaloacetate. Because the first stable product has four carbons, the pathway is called C4. PEP carboxylase has a high affinity for carbon dioxide and does not react with oxygen, so it works well even when the stomata are partly closed. The four-carbon acid is converted to malate or aspartate and is moved into the bundle sheath cells, where it is broken down to release carbon dioxide. This pumps up the carbon dioxide concentration around RuBisCO to several times the normal level, so that RuBisCO almost always meets carbon dioxide rather than oxygen. The Calvin cycle then runs in the bundle sheath cells. The three-carbon remnant returns to the mesophyll, where it is converted back to phosphoenolpyruvate. The extra cost pays off in hot, bright conditions, but is a disadvantage in cool, shady ones. C4 plants have an optimum temperature of about 30 to 40 degrees Celsius, and their photosynthesis does not saturate even in full sunlight. Because C4 plants can fix carbon dioxide efficiently with their stomata only partly open, they lose less water for each gram of dry matter they make. Typical figures are that a C4 plant may use around 250 to 350 grams of water per gram of dry matter, while a C3 plant uses roughly 450 to 950 grams. That is why maize and sugarcane thrive in warm regions where the sun is strong. CAM photosynthesis is the strategy of plants in very dry environments. CAM plants do not separate the two steps in space, as C4 plants do, but in time. At night, when the air is cool and humid, the stomata open. Carbon dioxide enters the leaf and is captured by PEP carboxylase, forming oxaloacetate, which is converted to malate. The malate is stored as malic acid in the large central vacuole of the cell. As a result the cells become measurably more acidic by morning, which is a hallmark of CAM. During the day, the stomata close tightly to prevent loss of water. The malate leaves the vacuole and is broken down to release carbon dioxide inside the cell, where RuBisCO and the Calvin cycle use it with the help of ATP and NADPH from the light reactions, which operate in sunlight.

This allows the plant to photosynthesize with its stomata shut during the heat of the day. CAM plants typically lose only a small amount of water, in the range of about 50 to 100 grams for each gram of dry matter. The price is slow growth, because the amount of carbon dioxide that can be stored in the vacuole at night is limited. This is why cacti and agaves grow slowly compared with maize. A comparison of the three pathways is useful. The first enzyme to capture carbon dioxide is RuBisCO in C3 plants and PEP carboxylase in both C4 and CAM plants. The Calvin cycle occurs in mesophyll cells in C3 plants, in bundle sheath cells in C4 plants, and in the same cells as the night-time capture in CAM plants. Climate and evolution shape the distribution of these plants. C4 photosynthesis evolved independently many times, more than sixty separate times, beginning about 30 million years ago when atmospheric carbon dioxide had declined. The spread of C4 grasslands about 6 to 8 million years ago is thought to have influenced the diets of grazing animals, including early human ancestors. CAM has also evolved many times, and some plants can switch between CAM and C3 depending on the amount of available water. The stable isotopes of carbon provide a way to tell

RuBisCO discriminates against the heavier carbon-13 more than PEP carboxylase does, so C3 plants contain proportionately less carbon-13 than C4 plants, with CAM plants falling somewhere in between. Scientists use this fact to study ancient diets, because the carbon isotope ratio of an animal's bones and teeth reflects whether it ate mostly C3 or C4 plants. Crop science makes use of these differences. Because C4 crops are so efficient, researchers have tried to engineer the C4 pathway into rice, a C3 crop, in the hope of raising yields by up to half. Another approach is to modify photorespiration in C3 crops so that the wasteful byproducts are recycled faster, and field trials in tobacco have shown that this can increase growth. Climate change affects the three types differently. Rising carbon dioxide gives C3 plants a bigger advantage, since it suppresses photorespiration and gives RuBisCO more carbon dioxide to work with, while C4 plants already concentrate carbon dioxide and benefit less. Higher temperatures and drought, on the other hand, tend to favor C4 and CAM plants. In many places the net effect depends on local conditions. The pathways differ only in how carbon dioxide is delivered to RuBisCO. Respiration, by contrast, takes place in the mitochondria and releases carbon dioxide rather than consuming it. In a leaf during the day, the rate of photosynthesis normally far exceeds the rate of respiration, so the plant is a net consumer of carbon dioxide. At night, without light, only respiration continues, and the plant releases carbon dioxide, with the exception of CAM plants, which take in carbon dioxide at night while their stomata are open. The details of photorespiration show why it is so costly. The plant must salvage the carbon through a series of reactions that occur in three organelles, the chloroplast, the peroxisome, and the mitochondrion. The salvage pathway releases carbon dioxide and consumes ATP, and it loses ammonia that must be recaptured. In a hot dry day the loss can be a large portion of what was just fixed. RuBisCO evolved when the atmosphere contained little oxygen and much more carbon dioxide, which explains why it handles oxygen so poorly. It is also a very slow enzyme, handling only about three molecules of carbon dioxide per second, so plants have to make huge amounts of it. Wheat and rice are grown widely in temperate and subtropical regions and rely on C3 photosynthesis. Maize, sugarcane, and sorghum are C4 crops whose yields are among the highest of any cereals per hectare. Pineapple is the best-known CAM crop, and farmers can plant it in dry soil because its leaves lose so little water. Agave is grown for tequila and fiber and thrives in desert land. The weed crabgrass, a C4 plant, tends to take over lawns in midsummer when cool-season C3 grasses such as bluegrass are stressed by heat, and this is why lawn care advice differs by season. Cellular respiration, mitosis, and meiosis PART ONE: CELLULAR RESPIRATION Cellular respiration is the set of reactions by which cells extract energy from food molecules and store it in a form that can be used for work. The most common fuel is glucose. In the presence of oxygen, one molecule of glucose is broken down to carbon dioxide and water, and the energy released is used to make adenosine triphosphate, or ATP, the main energy currency of the cell. In its simplest form the overall reaction is the reverse of photosynthesis: glucose plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide plus water plus energy. Respiration occurs in nearly all living cells, in plants as well as animals, and it happens day and night. Plants do not rely on photosynthesis alone, because the sugars they make must still be burned in respiration to power growth and transport. Respiration has four main stages: glycolysis, pyruvate

ust still be burned in respiration to power growth and transport. Respiration has four main stages: glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, the citric acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation. The first stage takes place in the cytosol, the fluid part of the cell outside the organelles, while the last three take place inside the mitochondria. This division of labor reflects the evolutionary history of the mitochondrion, which is thought to descend from a free-living bacterium that was engulfed by an ancestor of modern cells. Mitochondria are surrounded by two membranes, have their own small circular DNA, and divide independently of the cell. The inner membrane is folded into ridges called cristae, which increase the surface area available for the electron transport machinery. The fluid inside the inner membrane is called the matrix. It is a sequence of ten enzyme-catalyzed steps that converts one six-carbon glucose molecule into two three-carbon molecules of pyruvate. The first step is carried out by the enzyme hexokinase, which adds a phosphate group to glucose and traps it inside the cell. The step that is most important for regulation is catalyzed by phosphofructokinase, an enzyme that is slowed down when ATP is abundant and sped up when ATP is scarce, so that the cell burns sugar in proportion to its need.
